overview: This record represents Burma under the Konbaung dynasty, founded in 1752, rather than every people or kingdom of present-day Myanmar. Its imported dates, 1783 to 1878, cover only part of the dynasty. The outline also keeps southern territory long after British conquests in 1826 and 1852-53, so it should not be read as an accurate border for every selected year. The monarchy survived until the British invasion of 1885.

periods.title: Foundation and imperial expansion
periods.summary: Alaungpaya built a new dynasty from Shwebo. Expansion made the kingdom a major mainland power; wars displaced people as well as changing political control.

periods.title: Two wars and a shrinking kingdom
periods.summary: War with British India in 1824-26 cost the kingdom western and southern territories. A second war in 1852-53 brought the lower Irrawaddy valley under British control.

periods.title: Mindon and Mandalay
periods.summary: Mindon ruled the remaining kingdom, established his new capital at Mandalay and sponsored the carving of Buddhist scriptures onto marble.

periods.title: Thibaw and the end of the monarchy
periods.summary: Thibaw’s final reign ended with British occupation of Mandalay in 1885. Upper Burma was annexed in 1886; armed resistance continued afterward.

sections.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders

items.text: The dynasty began with U Aungzeya, better known as Alaungpaya, who organized resistance from Shwebo in 1752. Shwebo was also called Konbaung, the name later given to his dynasty. His victories over the southern Mon kingdom established a new royal house; the map’s 1783 starting point comes decades into that story.

Conquest moved skills and stories under brutal circumstances. After Burmese armies sacked Ayutthaya in 1767, large numbers of people were taken to central Myanmar. Thai theatrical performers helped popularize the Ramayana at the Burmese court, and travelling actors spread its stories more widely. Artistic exchange here was bound up with forced displacement.

Shan rulers were not simply provincial officials inside a tidy national border. Some paid tribute to Burmese kings and hosted soldiers; others had only nominal obligations. A state could acknowledge Burma, China or Siam at the same time. These overlapping relationships help explain why a single solid outline can exaggerate a king’s everyday control.

In 1882, after this map record ends, Thibaw issued two gold-foil commissions appointing Twek Nga Lu over Mong Nai and Kengtawng. The surviving documents carry royal seals. Their troubled history, amid rebellion and competing claimants, reveals how the court tried to turn a royal appointment into authority on the ground.

Rank could determine which objects and buildings an official was allowed to use. A painted folding book from about 1880, associated with minister U Shwe Maung, recorded such privileges. The British Museum interprets it as a guide issued after his promotion. His new job therefore came with an illustrated guide to its visible signs of status.

sections.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry

items.text: Alaungpaya sent George II an extraordinary letter in 1756, engraved on gold and decorated with rubies. It offered a site for English ships at Pathein and proposed friendship between their descendants. The letter travelled inside an ivory container, with further wrappings and boxes: diplomacy came with quite a lot of packaging.

A tiny Burmese sample from that Golden Letter is ဆင်ဖြူ, meaning “white elephants.” It occurs in the second line among the king’s claims to precious resources and magnificent animals. Historian Jacques Leider supplies both the Burmese transcript and an English translation. This is royal ceremonial language from a surviving 1756 document.

At Mandalay, Mindon’s scripture project produced a library whose pages were stone. Craftsmen carved the Buddhist Pali canon in Burmese script onto 729 marble slabs, completed in 1868 and housed in individual shrines. The language and alphabet are different things: these particular texts are Pali, even though their letters are Burmese.

Making that stone book required both scholarship and patient handwork. Senior monks and officials checked palm-leaf texts before the lettering was cut. The nomination records a carver completing roughly ten to twelve lines in a day. A spelling correction was considerably less convenient than reaching for an eraser.

Buddhist monasteries taught boys and helped sustain a strong tradition of literacy. Education also reached outward during Mindon’s reign: members of the royal family sent children to schools in India and farther afield, supported English-language newspapers, and explored science and technology. Royal schooling and village monastic learning offered very different kinds of opportunity.

sections.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things

items.text: A son entering a monastery could be an important family occasion. Relatives commissioned a decorated Kammavaca manuscript as a gift and an act of religious merit. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century examples survive on lacquered and gilded palm leaves. The ordination texts are Pali written in Burmese script, linking family generosity with the community’s religious learning.

Burmese folding-book paintings show chinlone players entertaining a royal audience while musicians perform nearby. The ball is woven from cane or rattan, and the challenge is to keep it airborne without using the hands. One painted performer handles three balls. It is a striking reminder that impressive footwork could be entertainment as well as exercise.

A Shan women’s lacquer box dated about 1840-1850 has two shallow trays above a deeper compartment, for jewellery, cosmetics or small clothing. Its painted story includes horsemen, swordsmen and a woman archer. The container organized possessions while putting a lively miniature drama around its sides.

A small Shan lacquered basket from about 1850 probably held betel-chewing ingredients. Its compact size suited personal use; larger containers served groups. The inside tray even hides an ogre in the decoration. A useful everyday object could reward a closer look after its lid was lifted.

Another lacquer set, made about 1850-1865, contains six boxes nested inside one another and a tray. Cylindrical containers commonly stored betel ingredients or pickled tea, but this particular arrangement may have been intended for European customers. Its uncertainty is interesting: the shape survives, while the original owner’s precise habits do not.

Medical learning also lived in books. A Burmese manuscript dated 1878 gathers seven medical works on 255 palm-leaf folios, with nine lines of writing on each side. Its edges and binding boards are gilded. This substantial, carefully protected collection shows sustained investment in recording medical knowledge; the catalogue does not establish whether its treatments worked.

The late kingdom shared the region with expanding British possessions. The 1826 settlement removed Arakan and Tenasserim from royal control; the war of 1852-53 brought British rule to the lower Irrawaddy. Upper Burma remained a separate monarchy until 1885. The coastal areas inside this atlas outline were therefore no longer all governed from the Burmese court.

The fall of the palace did not instantly settle the country. After Thibaw’s removal, resistance continued across Upper Burma and the Shan, Kachin and Chin hills. British officers then tried to convert former tributary relationships into colonial territorial borders, discovering that some rulers had acknowledged more than one powerful neighbour.

ending.text: British forces took Mandalay in November 1885 and exiled Thibaw and his family to India. Annexation of Upper Burma followed in 1886, ending the Konbaung monarchy. The imported 1878 cutoff is not that ending. Burmese and neighbouring communities continued under colonial rule, and armed resistance outlasted the loss of the court.
